The wind on the Isle of Solitude did not merely blow; it screamed. It was a high, thin keen that seemed to drill through the very bones of the granite cliffs, a sound that had defined the existence of Elias Thorne for thirty-seven years.

Elias was Lighthouse Keeper #0.

The title was not a rank, nor was it a number in a sequence. It was a designation given to him by the maritime authority in the year 1994, a time when the lighthouse was still considered a critical, albeit obsolete, piece of infrastructure. They had numbered the other keepers on the coast: #1 through #12, each managing their respective towers. But the Isle of Solitude was different. It was older than the coast, older than the nation itself. Its rock was black, volcanic, and jagged, jutting out of the North Sea like a broken tooth. The lighthouse atop it was not white, as was tradition, but a deep, charcoal grey, blending so seamlessly with the storm clouds that sailors often mistook it for a natural formation until the light swept the darkness.

Because the island was so remote, and because the light had never once failed in its history—no matter the storm, no matter the age of the keeper who tended it—the authorities had deemed it "Zero." The origin point. The anchor. If the light went out, the world would lose its way.

Elias was seventy-two years old now. His hair was a shock of white that whipped against his face like sea spray. His hands were mapped with scars from rope burns and frostbite, and his eyes,

The wind did not howl at the Edge of the World; it whispered. It was a low, constant susurrus that seemed to come from inside the rock itself, a reminder that the earth here was old, tired, and keeping secrets.

Elara Vance had been Lighthouse Keeper #0 for three years, six months, and four days.

The designation was not official in the maritime registry. In the logs of the Coastal Authority, she was simply "Vance, E. – Station 44: The Spire." But the other keepers, the ones on the mainland or the larger islands, knew the truth. There were no numbers before zero. There was no Keeper #1 who had laid the foundation, nor #2 who had first lit the great Fresnel lens. The Spire had always been there, and Elara had always been there. Or so it felt.

Her memory of the time before the Spire was a watercolor painting left out in the rain. She remembered her mother’s hands, flour-dusted and warm. She remembered the smell of ozone before a storm. But the dates were blurred. The years before she took the post dissolved into a grey mist, indistinguishable from the fog that rolled in from the Atlantic every night at 4:00 PM.

Today was the anniversary of her appointment. The Authority sent a supply boat once a month, a rusted-hulled vessel called *The Mule*, piloted by a man named Silas who never made eye contact. He dropped crates of tinned food, kerosene, and spare wicks at the base of the cliff, and he left. He never asked how she was. He never asked why she stayed.
